discussion_comments.comment_body: This requires an extra pass, which we should avoid.
This can be avoided by returning number of seen items in the debug case, in the non debug case we calculate as before but it's not a duplicate call

While the cache is `UNKNOWN`, this inserts an entry even for a local that hasn't been bound yet. A debugger enumerating locals on function entry can hit this with most slots still empty. I measured the first `len(proxy)` on a generator suspended at its first `yield`, with one bound argument and 256 unbound locals. The median went from 149 ns on the parent to 6,239 ns on this PR, and peak traced allocation during the call went from 216 to 9,776 bytes. I used matched GIL-enabled macOS arm64 release builds, seven runs per revision, and a fresh code object for each first read. Frame and proxy creation were outside the timer.

Could we track just the bound names on a sparse walk, mark `NEEDED` if two of them match, and otherwise leave the cache `UNKNOWN` until a walk can establish uniqueness?
Yes, I had that initially but then tried to be too clever. I'll do that.
Well, not exactly that but I had a separate one-time scan to decide dedup based on the names so everything else is simple.
I changed it to what you suggested. So it's optimised for the sparse case now. Does that make sense?

Once the cache says `NEEDED`, we skip unbound slots, so every value we put in this dict is `True`. Could we keep the old set of bound names for that case and only write `NEEDED` when we first discover a duplicate?

I timed repeated reads inside `[probe(sys._getframe().f_locals) for x in x]`, with 14 bound arguments plus the comprehension target and the enclosing `x`. Both `x` slots were live. These are median times per call over seven runs per revision on GIL-enabled macOS arm64 release builds.

| Call | PR parent | This PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `len(proxy)` | 191 ns | 345 ns |
| `proxy.keys()` | 239 ns | 390 ns |
| `proxy.values()` | 243 ns | 391 ns |
| `proxy.items()` | 346 ns | 507 ns |

Changing only the target to `y` gives 16 unique names and shows the intended speedup for `len(proxy)`, from 198 ns to 25 ns.

I wonder if we need to do any compilation performance testing of this PR on release builds? We are now doing this set allocation and per-name deduplication for every frame, including ordinary functions with no comprehensions, cells, or free variables. (Same for `values()`, `items()`, and `len()`.)

If this cost is totally invisible in real workloads, maybe this is fine and we just keep the code simpler. But it also seems quite feasible to limit the duplicate-tracking cost to code objects that could actually be affected by it.
Good point, though I think this code impacts introspection tools rather than the compiler. Let me see if it's easy to optimize.
Doable, but not trivial. I'd like to defer the optimisation to a separate PR.
